title: What If the Moon Were at the ISS's Height?
altTitles: What If the Moon Orbited 400 km Above Us?
The Moon, 400 km Away (This Is What Happens)
description: If the Moon orbited at the Space Station's height, tides would grow ~92,000x, and the Moon would crack inside Earth's Roche limit and become a ring. Speculative simulation grounded in real physics. Sources in pinned comment. #whatif #space #moon
topic: What if the Moon orbited at ISS height (400 km)

sections.label: B1 Hook

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Moon. Four hundred kilometers above your head.

sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal dusk shot: an enormous gibbous Moon filling the top seventy percent of the frame, craters razor-sharp, lit from the left with its terminator curving on the right, a flat dark horizon in the bottom fifth with one tiny human figure seen from behind for scale, deep blue sky. Camera: continuous slow push-in. STAGE: the Moon impossibly close, its disc spanning almost half the sky, grey cratered surface in sharp detail, lit from frame-left with its terminator visible; Earth otherwise as today.

sfx.prompt: deep cinematic sub-bass boom, single hit, then silence

sections.label: B2a Orbital

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That's the height of the Space Station. From here, the Moon would stretch across almost half the sky — and it wouldn't hang still. It would race around Earth in about two hours.

sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal orbital view: Earth's curved limb across the bottom third, the Moon skimming impossibly low just above the atmosphere, both lit from frame-left. Camera: continuous slow rise.

sections.label: B2b Time-lapse
sections.videoPrompt: Vertical locked-off time-lapse from the ground: the giant Moon sliding rapidly across the sky from left to right over a flat horizon, shadows swinging. Single-shot.

sfx.prompt: huge deep airy whoosh of a massive object passing overhead

sections.label: B3a Water dome

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now the real problem: tides. Tidal pull grows with the cube of closeness. Bring the Moon forty-five times closer, and its tidal stretch on Earth grows about ninety thousand times. Oceans heave into a moving mountain of water. Even the crust flexes.

sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal wide shot from high cliffs over a generic open ocean coast, the sea surface bulging upward into a colossal smooth dome of water rising toward the giant Moon above, no people, no buildings. Camera: continuous slow tilt-up from water to Moon. STAGE: the Moon impossibly close, its disc spanning almost half the sky, grey cratered surface in sharp detail, lit from frame-left with its terminator visible; Earth otherwise as today.

sfx.prompt: deep rising ocean roar, massive swell of water, rumbling

sections.label: B3b Crust
sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal aerial of a generic desert plain splitting along a long glowing fissure, dust rising, the giant Moon above. Camera: continuous slow descent. STAGE: the Moon impossibly close, its disc spanning almost half the sky, grey cratered surface in sharp detail, lit from frame-left with its terminator visible; Earth otherwise as today.

sfx.prompt: deep ground crack and rock splitting, low earthquake rumble

sections.label: B4a Moon cracks

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And it works both ways. At this distance, the Moon is deep inside Earth's Roche limit — where tides beat a moon's own gravity. So the Moon doesn't crash. It cracks. It stretches, splits, and shatters.

sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal orbital view of the Moon, very close above Earth's limb, stretched slightly into an egg shape, long glowing fractures opening across its surface, lit from frame-left. Camera: continuous slow push. STAGE: the Moon impossibly close, its disc spanning almost half the sky, grey cratered surface in sharp detail, lit from frame-left with its terminator visible; Earth otherwise as today.

sfx.prompt: single colossal rock crack followed by a long deep rumble in space

labels.text: ROCHE LIMIT ≈ 18,000 km · MOON AT ≈ 8,500 km

sections.label: B4b Fragments
sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal orbital view: the fractured Moon continuing to separate into huge tumbling fragments drifting apart along its orbit, dust glittering, Earth's limb below. Camera: continuous slow push. STAGE: the Moon impossibly close, its disc spanning almost half the sky, grey cratered surface in sharp detail, lit from frame-left with its terminator visible; Earth otherwise as today.

sections.label: B5a Ring forms

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fragments keep orbiting — spreading out, colliding, flattening into a disk around the equator. Within centuries: a ring. Grey rock, catching the sunlight, arching over every horizon — and some of it raining down as meteors for ages.

sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal orbital view of Earth with a thin, flat grey-brown ring in its equatorial plane, lit from frame-left, city lights on the night side. Camera: continuous slow arc upward. STAGE: no Moon; a broad grey-brown rocky ring arch across the sky, lit from frame-left; Earth otherwise as today.

sfx.prompt: shimmering harp glint, magical and bright, single phrase

sections.label: B5b Ring arch
sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal dusk ground shot over the same flat horizon and tiny figure as the opening, a broad grey-gold ring arch spanning the sky above, deep blue sky. Camera: continuous slow tilt-down toward the figure. STAGE: no Moon; a broad grey-brown rocky ring arch across the sky, lit from frame-left; Earth otherwise as today.

sections.label: B6 Loop

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That's why the Moon can never be four hundred kilometers above your head.

sections.videoPrompt: Vertical photoreal dusk: the tiny figure on the flat horizon beneath the ring arch, framing identical to the opening shot's bottom fifth, sky above.
